|access-date=September 19, 2024 |website=The Mercury News |language=en-US}} A four-time CFL All-Star and four-time NFL [[Pro Bowl]] selection, Garcia began his professional football career with the CFL's [[Calgary Stampeders]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 1994. In 1999, Garcia debuted in the NFL with the [[San Francisco 49ers]]. With the 49ers, Garcia made three [[Pro Bowl]] appearances (for the [[2001 Pro Bowl|2000]], [[2002 Pro Bowl|2001]], and [[2003 Pro Bowl|2002 season]]s) and led the team to the playoffs in the [[2001 San Francisco 49ers season|2001]] and [[2002 San Francisco 49ers season|2002 season]]s. Afterwards, Garcia encountered a low point in his career, starting with a lackluster 2003 season with San Francisco then two losing seasons with the [[Cleveland Browns]] in 2004 and the [[Detroit Lions]] in 2005. With the [[Philadelphia Eagles]], Garcia returned to form late in the 2006 season, starting for an injured [[Donovan McNabb]] and leading Philadelphia to the playoffs. Garcia joined the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in 2007 and was the starting quarterback for most games of the 2007 and 2008 seasons. Again, Garcia led Tampa Bay to the playoffs in 2007 and made his fourth career [[2008 Pro Bowl|Pro Bowl]] appearance. After his stint with Tampa, Garcia returned to the Eagles in 2009 and played only one game. In 2010, Garcia played for the [[Omaha Nighthawks]] of the [[United Football League (2009)|United Football League]]. In 2011, Garcia signed with the [[Houston Texans]] but did not play a game with the team. The following year, Garcia joined the advisory board for the now defunct United States Football League.{{cite web | url=http://theusfl.com/usfl-announces-2015-kickoff-date | title=USFL Announces 2015 Kickoff Date | date=September 13, 2013 | publisher=United States Football League | access-date=September 30, 2013 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131006015719/http://theusfl.com/usfl-announces-2015-kickoff-date/ | archive-date=October 6, 2013}}

'''Jeffrey Alan Hartings''' (born September 7, 1972) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Center (American football)|center]] for 11 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Penn State Nittany Lions football|Penn State Nittany Lions]], earning [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors. A first-round pick of the [[Detroit Lions]] in the [[1996 NFL draft]], he played professionally for the Lions and [[Pittsburgh Steelers]]. He was a member of the Steelers' [[Super Bowl]] championship team in 2005, beating the [[Seattle Seahawks]], and he was a two-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection. He is currently the head football coach at [[Worthington Christian High School]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ulrey |first=Jarrod |date=April 19, 2017 |title=Football: Former NFL lineman named coach at Worthington Christian |url=https://www.dispatch.com/story/news/local/worthington/2017/04/19/football-former-nfl-lineman-named/21308267007/ |access-date=2024-05-24 |website=The Columbus Dispatch |language=en-US}}</ref>

USFL: {{Winning percentage|2|8|record=y}} | pfrcoach = FishJe0 }} '''Jeffrey Michael Fisher''' (born February 25, 1958) is an American professional [[American football|football]] coach, executive, and former [[cornerback]] and [[return specialist]]. He served as a head coach in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 22 seasons, primarily with the [[Houston Oilers|Houston]] / [[Tennessee Titans|Tennessee Oilers / Titans]] franchise. Fisher coached the Oilers / Titans from [[1994 Houston Oilers season|1994]] to [[2010 Tennessee Titans season|2010]] and the [[St. Louis Rams|St. Louis]] / [[Los Angeles Rams]] from [[2012 St. Louis Rams season|2012]] to [[2016 Los Angeles Rams season|2016]]. He is currently the commissioner of [[Arena Football One]], after serving as interim commissioner of the previous incarnation of the [[Arena Football League (2024)|Arena Football League]] and also majority owner of the AF1's [[Nashville Kats (2024)|Nashville Kats]]. After playing [[college football]] for the [[USC Trojans football|USC Trojans]], Fisher was drafted in the seventh round of the [[1981 NFL draft]] by the [[Chicago Bears]], and played with the Bears for five seasons. He won a [[Super Bowl ring]] in 1985 while on injured reserve during his final season as a player. Fisher then held several coaching positions for various teams before becoming the head coach of the Titans towards the end of the [[1994 NFL season|1994 season]] during their tenure as the Houston Oilers and was the team's first coach when they relocated to [[Tennessee]]. Fisher continued to coach the Titans until after the end of the 2010 season when he and the team mutually agreed to part ways. Following a season away from football, Fisher was hired as the head coach of the Rams in 2012 and coached the team during their last four years in [[St. Louis]]. He remained the head coach of the Rams during the franchise's return to Los Angeles in 2016 but was fired near the end of the season.{{Cite web |last=Gonzalez |first=Alden |date=December 12, 2016 |title=Jeff Fisher fired as Rams coach |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/18263718/jeff-fisher-fired-coach-st-louis-rams |access-date=December 12, 2016 |website=[[ESPN.com]]}} Fisher's most successful season was in [[1999 NFL season|1999]], when he led the Titans to the franchise's first (and only) [[Super Bowl]] appearance in [[Super Bowl XXXIV|XXXIV]], which ended in close defeat by the Rams for their first Super Bowl title. However, despite compiling a winning record as a head coach, Fisher's career has been noted for an overall lack of success, having only attained six winning seasons and postseason appearances in over two decades in the NFL. He is tied with [[Dan Reeves]] and [[Bill Belichick]] for the most regular-season losses in NFL history at 165, but has the third-most total losses at 171, behind Reeves at 174 and Belichick at 178.{{cite web|title=Blowout loss gives Jeff Fisher record-tying 165th career defeat|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/18258658/los-angeles-rams-coach-jeff-fisher-ties-nfl-record-165th-career-loss|work=ESPN|date=December 12, 2016|first=Alden|last= Gonzalez}}

'''Jeffrey Scott George''' (born December 8, 1967) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 14 seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Illinois Fighting Illini]], earning the [[Sammy Baugh Trophy]] and first-team [[List of All-Big Ten Conference football teams|All-Big Ten]] honors in 1989.

George was selected [[list of first overall National Football League Draft picks|first overall]] by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the [[1990 NFL draft]]. A member of seven NFL teams, he helped the [[Atlanta Falcons]] in 1995 and the [[Minnesota Vikings]] in 1999 reach the playoffs and led the league in passing yards in 1997 with the [[Oakland Raiders]]. George's NFL career would also be marked by frequent conflicts with coaches and management, which resulted in his departure from most of his teams.

'''Jeffrey Allan Feagles''' (born March 7, 1966) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Punter (gridiron football)|punter]] for 22 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]]. He was originally signed by the [[New England Patriots]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 1988, and retired in 2010 after last playing for the [[New York Giants]].

Feagles is known for using the "[[Coffin corner (American football)|coffin corner]]" punt. He earned [[Pro Bowl]] selections in [[1996 Pro Bowl|1995]] and [[2009 Pro Bowl|2008]] and won a [[Super Bowl ring]] with the Giants in [[Super Bowl XLII]] over the Patriots. In his 22-season career, Feagles never missed a game, a record amongst [[American_football_positions#Special_teams|special teams]] players.

'''Jeffrey Clyde Hayes''' (born August 19, 1959) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Punter (American football)|punter]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Washington Redskins]], [[Cincinnati Bengals]], and the [[Miami Dolphins]]. He scored one touchdown, running for a 61-yard touchdown while playing for the Bengals against the Pittsburgh Steelers via a fake punt where he evaded two tackles. While playing for Washington, he made four rushing attempts that included a 24-yard run in 1984 following a 48-yard run in 1983. He finished his career with 168 rushing yards from 7 attempts.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Huff |first1=Donald |title=Hayes' Fakes Are Off and Running |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1983/11/03/hayes-fakes-are-off-and-running/864b242c-19c2-43a6-9a0a-7d670715cbe2/ |newspaper=[[Washington Post]] |date=1983-11-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Jeff Hayes Career Stats |url=https://www.nfl.com/players/jeff-hayes/stats/career |website=NFL.com}}</ref> His 61-yard run is the longest touchdown run for a kicker or punter, and was the longest run for those positions until [[Reggie Hodges]]'s 68 yard, non-touchdown run in a 2010 game against the [[New Orleans Saints]].

'''Jeffrey Lance Gooch''' (born October 31, 1974) is a [[linebacker]] who played for 10 seasons for the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] and [[Detroit Lions]] in the [[National Football League]].

Gooch played at [[John Overton Comprehensive High School|John Overton High School]] in Nashville, Tennessee and finished his career there with 215 tackles.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://admin.xosn.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=85760&SPID=10135&DB_OEM_ID=16900&ATCLID=1377578 |title=Hall of Fame - Jeff Gooch |access-date=2008-11-15 |archive-date=2012-09-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120919143757/https://admin.xosn.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=85760&SPID=10135&DB_OEM_ID=16900&ATCLID=1377578 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  Gooch went undrafted in the [[1996 NFL draft]] out of [[Austin Peay State University]]. He was later signed by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] as an undrafted free agent. His rookie year, he appeared in 15 games for the Buccaneers, mostly on special teams. In 1997, he played in all 16 games while starting 5 of them. In 1998, Gooch registered his first career sack in a 24–22 victory over the [[Green Bay Packers]] as he started all 16 games and recorded 62 tackles. From 1999 to 2001, Gooch played in 44 out of 48 games, but he recorded only 65 tackles in the three seasons combined. In 2002, he left the Buccaneers to sign with the Detroit Lions where he played in all 16 games in both years with the team (2002–2003), while watching the Buccaneers win a [[Super Bowl XXXVII|Super Bowl]] before he returned to play his final season with the team.  He later served as the Vice President of Football Operations for the [[Tampa Bay Storm]] of the [[Arena Football League]].
